notes.1a: Most candidates correctly identified YZ as the decelerating section and XY as the constant speed section of the speed time graph.
notes.1b: Most candidates correctly used the area under the graph or average speed ⋅ time to calculate distance. Weaker candidates attempted to use the speed formula but did not use average speed. Correct answer 400 (m).
notes.1c: The strongest candidates gave the steeper gradient as their answer. Weaker candidates stated that less time was spent accelerating than decelerating, which was insufficient without an indication that the speed change was the same.
notes.2a: Most of the stronger candidates correctly identified the units as kg, m, m . Weaker candidates often gave g, cm, cm .
notes.2bi: The majority of candidates correctly calculated weight. A minority divided mass by 10. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2018 (ii) Most stronger candidates used the pressure formula correctly. Some candidates could not recall the correct formula. Others overlooked the fact that there were four feet. Some candidates did not give the correct unit for pressure.
notes.3a: Only stronger candidates were able to identify the manometer. Many other candidates stated that it was a barometer.
notes.3b: Stronger candidates were able to make the link between air pressure and the difference in liquid levels.
notes.3c: This question was challenging for many candidates. Many stated that level A would go down and level B would go up. Some commented on pressure change but did not state what would happen to the levels.
notes.4a: Many candidates gave good answers. Some candidates used the term “potential” energy for the first part without specifying it was chemical.
notes.4b: Many candidates struggled to link a large quantity of potential energy with height and small quantity of kinetic energy with low speed.
notes.4c: Only the strongest candidates identified the wasted energy and what happened to it.
notes.5a: Only a few of the strongest candidates understood the term thermal capacity.
notes.5b: Almost all candidates demonstrated excellent knowledge of the phase changes.
notes.5c: Many candidates stated the pressure would increase but fewer went on to explain this in terms of the increased kinetic energy of the molecules and more frequent/harder collisions with the container.
notes.6ai: Many candidates found it challenging to determine the correct direction of the refracted ray at each surface. Normals were often drawn at angles other than at 90° to the surface.
notes.6aii: Stronger candidates answered this well but weaker candidates found it more of a challenge with diffraction and reflection amongst the more frequently seen incorrect answers.
notes.6b: Most candidates correctly showed the rays converging and intersecting.
notes.7a: Most candidates correctly identified the colours of the spectrum and placed them in the correct sequence.
notes.7bi: Most candidates linked the use to the correct type of radiation. The most frequent error was linking the detection of an intruder at night with visible light.
notes.8a: Most candidates correctly identified 20 Hz–20 000 Hz as the range for a healthy human ear. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2018 (b) Only stronger candidates correctly explained that the term ultrasound was about frequencies above 20 000 Hz. A significant number of candidates described the uses of ultrasound.
notes.8c: Many candidates identified sound P as having smaller amplitude and lower frequency. A minority went on to link this to a quieter and lower pitch sound.
notes.9a: Most candidates correctly mentioned a magnetic field. Many stronger candidates went on to say this was changing, resulting in an induced voltage/current.
notes.9b: Most candidates identified at least one way to increase the brightness. Most of the stronger candidates were able to identify three ways.
notes.9ci: Only the strongest candidates were able to correctly give the answer “alternating current”. Many candidates put “alternative current” or described what it was.
notes.9cii: Most of the stronger candidates were able to describe how a.c differs from d.c.
notes.10a: Most candidates correctly named the variable resistor.
notes.10b: Most candidates gave the correct current.
notes.10c: The vast majority of candidates correctly calculated the resistance.
notes.10d: Although many candidates stated the correct relationship between resistance and current, many stated that a thicker wire would have less current. Stronger candidates correctly stated that there would be more current through the thicker wire.
notes.11a: Most candidates correctly drew two circles with a clockwise arrow.
notes.11b: Most of the stronger candidates gave a good description of how the bell worked. Weaker candidates just described the flow of current round the circuit.
notes.12a: The vast majority of candidates matched the parts of the atom to the correct descriptions.
notes.12bi: Most candidates correctly stated that an isotope has the same number of protons but different number of neutrons.
notes.12bii: Most candidates were able to take information from the graph and calculated the half-life. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2018
